threads_text: Microsoft just reported $92.3 billion in revenue for one quarter, its 10th record in a row, with Azure up 48%. It also spent a record $45.2 billion on capital expenditures, and the stock still rose after hours. Is Big Tech's AI spending finally paying off?
caption:
Microsoft reported $92.3 billion in revenue for the quarter that ended September 30, its 10th record quarter in a row.
Azure grew 48% to $33.2 billion, and capital spending hit a record $45.2 billion.
Shares rose about 5% in extended trading.

Is the AI spending boom finally paying off?

site_article.headline: Microsoft posts record $92.3 billion quarter as Azure growth speeds up to 48 percent
site_article.dek: Capital spending also hit a record $45.2 billion, and Microsoft reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI.
site_article.summary: Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for its fiscal first quarter on October 28, 2026, up 19 percent from a year earlier and its 10th record quarter in a row. Azure revenue rose 48 percent to $33.2 billion, while capital expenditures reached a record $45.2 billion.
site_article.seo_title: Microsoft Q1 earnings: $92.3B revenue, Azure up 48 percent
site_article.seo_description: Microsoft reported record revenue of $92.3 billion, Azure growth of 48 percent and record capital spending of $45.2 billion on October 28, 2026.
site_article.answer_summary: Microsoft earned $92.3 billion in revenue in the quarter that ended September 30, 2026, a record, driven by 48 percent growth in Azure. Shares rose about 5 percent in extended trading.
site_article.hero_alt: Photo of Microsoft chief executive Satya Nadella.

paragraphs.text: Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for its fiscal first quarter, which ended September 30, 2026, the company said on Wednesday, October 28. That was up 19 percent from a year earlier and marked the company's 10th consecutive quarter of record revenue, according to TechCrunch.

The result came in above Wall Street's expectations. Analysts polled by LSEG had forecast about $90.69 billion in revenue, Calcalist reported. Adjusted earnings per share were $4.89, compared with the $4.73 analysts expected, a figure that excludes the effect of Microsoft's investments in OpenAI. Net income rose 32 percent to $36.6 billion on a GAAP basis, according to TechCrunch.

Azure, the company's cloud computing platform, generated $33.17 billion in revenue, an increase of 48 percent from a year earlier. Growth accelerated from 42 percent in the previous quarter and beat analyst estimates, according to Calcalist. TechCrunch noted that not all Azure revenue is tied to AI.

The broader Microsoft Cloud business brought in $63.9 billion, up 30 percent, and Microsoft 365 contributed nearly $28 billion, TechCrunch reported. Microsoft also reported $10 billion in revenue from OpenAI. TechCrunch noted that OpenAI still runs many of its services on Microsoft's cloud even though it also uses Amazon Web Services, Oracle and other providers, and that Anthropic runs on Azure as well.
Commercial remaining performance obligation, a measure of contracted revenue that has not yet been recognized, rose 73 percent to $677 billion, according to TechCrunch.
Record spending and weaker cash flow

Capital expenditures, including finance leases, totaled $45.2 billion in the quarter, an all-time quarterly record for the company. Calcalist reported that the figure was up about 30 percent from a year earlier but below the $50.67 billion that analysts surveyed by StreetAccount had projected. Free cash flow fell 27 percent to $18.63 billion.

Not every part of the business grew. Revenue in Devices and Consumer was $15.5 billion, down 3 percent, and Windows OEM and devices revenue fell 22 percent from a year earlier, according to TechCrunch. Microsoft has reorganized its reporting into two segments, Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.
Investors responded positively. Microsoft shares rose about 5 percent in extended trading after the results were released, Calcalist reported.

In NeuraFeed's reading, the quarter shows the two sides of the AI build out at Microsoft. Cloud demand is growing faster than it was three months ago, and contracted future revenue is far larger than a year ago, which suggests customers are committing to long term AI workloads. At the same time, record capital spending is pulling down free cash flow, so the company is still paying heavily up front for capacity that will be earned back over years. The size of the OpenAI figure also shows how closely Microsoft's results remain tied to a single partner.

The next thing to watch is whether Azure can keep growing above 40 percent while capital spending keeps rising, since that balance will decide whether investors stay comfortable with the cost of Microsoft's AI expansion.
